ruleList.ruleOverview: NP: Parameter must be non-null but is marked as nullable
ruleList.desc: This parameter is always used in a way that requires it to be non-null, but the parameter is explicitly annotated as being Nullable. Either the use of the parameter or the annotation is wrong.

ruleList.ruleOverview: NP: Possible null pointer dereference due to return value of called method
ruleList.desc: The return value from a method is dereferenced without a null check, and the return value of that method is one that should generally be checked for null. This may lead to a NullPointerException when the code is executed.

ruleList.ruleOverview: NP: Possible null pointer dereference on branch that might be infeasible
ruleList.desc: There is a branch of statement that, if executed, guarantees that a null value will be dereferenced, which would generate a NullPointerException when the code is executed. Of course, the problem might be that the branch or statement is infeasible and that the null pointer exception cannot ever be executed; deciding that is beyond the ability of SpotBugs. Due to the fact that this value had been previously tested for nullness, this is a definite possibility.

ruleList.ruleOverview: NP: Load of known null value
ruleList.desc: The variable referenced at this point is known to be null due to an earlier check against null. Although this is valid, it might be a mistake (perhaps you intended to refer to a different variable, or perhaps the earlier check to see if the variable is null should have been a check to see if it was non-null).

ruleList.ruleOverview: PZLA: Consider returning a zero length array rather than null
ruleList.desc: It is often a better design to return a length zero array rather than a null reference to indicate that there are no results (i.e., an empty list of results). This way, no explicit check for null is needed by clients of the method.

ruleList.ruleOverview: UCF: Useless control flow
ruleList.desc: This method contains a useless control flow statement, where control flow continues onto the same place regardless of whether or not the branch is taken. For example, this is caused by having an empty statement block for an if statement:

ruleList.ruleOverview: UCF: Useless control flow to next line
ruleList.desc: This method contains a useless control flow statement in which control flow follows to the same or following line regardless of whether or not the branch is taken. Often, this is caused by inadvertently using an empty statement as the body of an if statement, e.g.:

ruleList.ruleOverview: RCN: Redundant nullcheck of value known to be null
ruleList.desc: This method contains a redundant check of a known null value against the constant null.

ruleList.ruleOverview: RCN: Redundant nullcheck of value known to be non-null
ruleList.desc: This method contains a redundant check of a known non-null value against the constant null.

ruleList.ruleOverview: RCN: Redundant comparison of two null values
ruleList.desc: This method contains a redundant comparison of two references known to both be definitely null.

ruleList.ruleOverview: RCN: Redundant comparison of non-null value to null
ruleList.desc: This method contains a reference known to be non-null with another reference known to be null.

ruleList.ruleOverview: SA: Self assignment of local variable
ruleList.desc: This method contains a self assignment of a local variable; e.g.

ruleList.ruleOverview: INT: Integer remainder modulo 1
ruleList.desc: Any expression (exp % 1) is guaranteed to always return zero. Did you mean (exp & 1) or (exp % 2) instead?

ruleList.ruleOverview: INT: Vacuous comparison of integer value
ruleList.desc: There is an integer comparison that always returns the same value (e.g., x <= Integer.MAX_VALUE).

ruleList.ruleOverview: INT: Vacuous bit mask operation on integer value
ruleList.desc: This is an integer bit operation (and, or, or exclusive or) that doesn't do any useful work (e.g., v & 0xffffffff).

ruleList.ruleOverview: SA: Double assignment of local variable
ruleList.desc: This method contains a double assignment of a local variable; e.g.

ruleList.ruleOverview: SA: Double assignment of field
ruleList.desc: This method contains a double assignment of a field; e.g.

ruleList.ruleOverview: DLS: Useless assignment in return statement
ruleList.desc: This statement assigns to a local variable in a return statement. This assignment has no effect. Please verify that this statement does the right thing.

ruleList.ruleOverview: DLS: Dead store to local variable
ruleList.desc: This instruction assigns a value to a local variable, but the value is not read or used in any subsequent instruction. Often, this indicates an error, because the value computed is never used.

ruleList.ruleOverview: DLS: Dead store to local variable that shadows field
ruleList.desc: This instruction assigns a value to a local variable, but the value is not read or used in any subsequent instruction. Often, this indicates an error, because the value computed is never used. There is a field with the same name as the local variable. Did you mean to assign to that variable instead?

ruleList.ruleOverview: DLS: Dead store of null to local variable
ruleList.desc: The code stores null into a local variable, and the stored value is not read. This store may have been introduced to assist the garbage collector, but as of Java SE 6.0, this is no longer needed or useful.

ruleList.ruleOverview: REC: Exception is caught when Exception is not thrown
ruleList.desc: This method uses a try-catch block that catches Exception objects, but Exception is not thrown within the try block, and RuntimeException is not explicitly caught. It is a common bug pattern to say try { ... } catch (Exception e) { something } as a shorthand for catching a number of types of exception each of whose catch blocks is identical, but this construct also accidentally catches RuntimeException as well, masking potential bugs.

ruleList.ruleOverview: DCN: NullPointerException caught
ruleList.desc: According to SEI Cert rule ERR08-J NullPointerException should not be caught. Handling NullPointerException is considered an inferior alternative to null-checking.

ruleList.ruleOverview: FE: Test for floating point equality
ruleList.desc: This operation compares two floating point values for equality. Because floating point calculations may involve rounding, calculated float and double values may not be accurate. For values that must be precise, such as monetary values, consider using a fixed-precision type such as BigDecimal. For values that need not be precise, consider comparing for equality within some range, for example: if ( Math.abs(x - y) < .0000001 ). See the Java Language Specification, section 4.2.4.

ruleList.ruleOverview: CD: Test for circular dependencies among classes
ruleList.desc: This class has a circular dependency with other classes. This makes building these classes difficult, as each is dependent on the other to build correctly. Consider using interfaces to break the hard dependency.

ruleList.ruleOverview: RI: Class implements same interface as superclass
ruleList.desc: This class declares that it implements an interface that is also implemented by a superclass. This is redundant because once a superclass implements an interface, all subclasses by default also implement this interface. It may point out that the inheritance hierarchy has changed since this class was created, and consideration should be given to the ownership of the interface's implementation.

ruleList.ruleOverview: MTIA: Class extends Struts Action class and uses instance variables
ruleList.desc: This class extends from a Struts Action class, and uses an instance member variable. Since only one instance of a struts Action class is created by the Struts framework, and used in a multithreaded way, this paradigm is highly discouraged and most likely problematic. Consider only using method local variables. Only instance fields that are written outside of a monitor are reported.

ruleList.ruleOverview: MTIA: Class extends Servlet class and uses instance variables
ruleList.desc: This class extends from a Servlet class, and uses an instance member variable. Since only one instance of a Servlet class is created by the J2EE framework, and used in a multithreaded way, this paradigm is highly discouraged and most likely problematic. Consider only using method local variables.

ruleList.ruleOverview: PS: Class exposes synchronization and semaphores in its public interface
ruleList.desc: This class uses synchronization along with wait(), notify() or notifyAll() on itself (the this reference). Client classes that use this class, may, in addition, use an instance of this class as a synchronizing object. Because two classes are using the same object for synchronization, Multithread correctness is suspect. You should not synchronize nor call semaphore methods on a public reference. Consider using an internal private member variable to control synchronization.

ruleList.ruleOverview: ICAST: Result of integer multiplication cast to long
ruleList.desc: This code performs integer multiply and then converts the result to a long, as in:

ruleList.ruleOverview: ICAST: Integral division result cast to double or float
ruleList.desc: This code casts the result of an integral division (e.g., int or long division) operation to double or float. Doing division on integers truncates the result to the integer value closest to zero. The fact that the result was cast to double suggests that this precision should have been retained. What was probably meant was to cast one or both of the operands to double before performing the division. Here is an example:

ruleList.ruleOverview: BC: Questionable cast to concrete collection
ruleList.desc: This code casts an abstract collection (such as a Collection, List, or Set) to a specific concrete implementation (such as an ArrayList or HashSet). This might not be correct, and it may make your code fragile, since it makes it harder to switch to other concrete implementations at a future point. Unless you have a particular reason to do so, just use the abstract collection class.

ruleList.ruleOverview: BC: Unchecked/unconfirmed cast
ruleList.desc: This cast is unchecked, and not all instances of the type cast from can be cast to the type it is being cast to. Check that your program logic ensures that this cast will not fail.

ruleList.ruleOverview: BC: Unchecked/unconfirmed cast of return value from method
ruleList.desc: This code performs an unchecked cast of the return value of a method. The code might be calling the method in such a way that the cast is guaranteed to be safe, but SpotBugs is unable to verify that the cast is safe. Check that your program logic ensures that this cast will not fail.

ruleList.ruleOverview: BC: instanceof will always return true
ruleList.desc: This instanceof test will always return true (unless the value being tested is null). Although this is safe, make sure it isn't an indication of some misunderstanding or some other logic error. If you really want to test the value for being null, perhaps it would be clearer to do better to do a null test rather than an instanceof test.

ruleList.ruleOverview: BC: Questionable cast to abstract collection
ruleList.desc: This code casts a Collection to an abstract collection (such as List, Set, or Map). Ensure that you are guaranteed that the object is of the type you are casting to. If all you need is to be able to iterate through a collection, you don't need to cast it to a Set or List.

ruleList.ruleOverview: IM: Check for oddness that won’t work for negative numbers
ruleList.desc: The code uses x % 2 == 1 to check to see if a value is odd, but this won't work for negative numbers (e.g., (-5) % 2 == -1). If this code is intending to check for oddness, consider using (x & 1) == 1, or x % 2 != 0.

ruleList.ruleOverview: IM: Computation of average could overflow
ruleList.desc: The code computes the average of two integers using either division or signed right shift, and then uses the result as the index of an array. If the values being averaged are very large, this can overflow (resulting in the computation of a negative average). Assuming that the result is intended to be nonnegative, you can use an unsigned right shift instead. In other words, rather that using (low+high)/2, use (low+high) >>> 1

ruleList.ruleOverview: BSHIFT: Unsigned right shift cast to short/byte
ruleList.desc: The code performs an unsigned right shift, whose result is then cast to a short or byte, which discards the upper bits of the result. Since the upper bits are discarded, there may be no difference between a signed and unsigned right shift (depending upon the size of the shift).

ruleList.ruleOverview: DMI: Code contains a hard coded reference to an absolute pathname
